On Monday, August 10, 2015 at 7:20:36 PM UTC+8, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I know that this is a "cold" thread but I would like to share some thoughts on this. We have done some work to fit unimplemented models in R-INLA by fitting several models with R-INLA where some parameters had been fixed (so that the model could be fitted with R-INLA) and then combining all the resulting models using Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA).
>
> The idea is that if we have a model that is not implemented in R-INLA but that could be fitted by fixing one or a few parameters, then we could take different values of this ensemble of parameters over a grid, fit the conditional models (on the values of these parameters) and then combine them together using BMA. If the model is already available in R-INLA it may be faster to run simpler models and then combine them, depending on the amount of data we have.
>
> I am not sure if this would qualify as a Map-Reduce algorithm. The Map part would be splitting the whole model into (simpler) conditional models and the Reduce step would be to put all the model outputs together to get the desired (and more complex) model.
>
> We have some code in the INLABMA that could me summarised as:
>
> #Define grid on nuisance parameter rho
> rrho<-seq(0, .95, length.out=40)
>
> #Fit condintioned models by fixing the value of rho
> #sem.inla() uses RINLA to fit a model given the value of rho
> #MAP step (?)
>
>  seminla<-mclapply(rrho, function(rho){
>                           sem.inla(form, d=columbus, W=W, rho=rho, ...)
>      })
>
> #Put all the models together to get our original model
> #REDUCE step (?)
> sembma<-INLABMA(seminla, rrho, 0)
>
>
> Conditional models are fitted in parallel using mclapply(). If data are distributed over different nodes, I do not think this approach could handle it, but it could deal with large datasets in one node because we are fitting simpler models. Combining the models only involves computing a weighted sum of matrices (e.g., the matrices representing the posterior marginals) and it can also be done very fast and in parallel.
>
> Not sure if this makes sense, but any comments on this are welcome.
>
> Best,
>
> Virgilio
>
> P.S: This approach is detailed in Bivand et al. (2014), Spatial Statistics journal. You can also check the INLABMA package to get the full example that I have mentioned.

> > > I am new to R-INLA. I have read the paper by Rue, Martino, and Chopin

> > > used in both R-INLA and the underlying GMRFlib. I get the gist of the
> > > method from the papers but I am at a disadvantage, being a computer
> > > scientist, in understanding the details of the algorithms and their
> > > implementation. I suspect I will have to read the source code and
> > > reverse engineer the architecture.
> > >
> > > I am interested in building a Bayesian model solver for big data
> > > sets. To make this concrete, let's start simple with Bayesian linear
> > > regression with a data set that has ten billion rows and a hundred
> > > real valuated covariates and ten thousand sparse indicator
> > > covariates. I just made up this example to given an example that will
> > > never fit in R. I am interested in studying INLA to see if it can be
> > > solved with the Map-Reduce paradigm use in Spark, an open source
> > > distributed computing system. Two areas where there are known
> > > parallel methods with Map-Reduce algorithms for big data sets are
> > > numerical linear algebra and convex optimization. I am interested in
> > > learning how INLA uses linear algebra and if the various optimization
> > > steps are convex optimization problems. One area that has been very
> > > useful for big data are randomized numerical linear algebra
> > > algorithms. These algorithms can invert a nxm matrix in O(n x m x
> > > log(m)). Being yet another approximation in the algorithms, it is
> > > unknown how the approximation error would propagate through the
> > > algorithms.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] coercing inla.mesh to Spatial* object
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] coercing inla.mesh to Spatial* object
messages.body_plain:
There is no SpatialTriangulation class unfortunately, so it would need to be a SpatialPolygons object. I never wrote such a converter, but we have implemented ggplot2 geoms for inla.mesh objects in the inlabru package; see the tutorials/workshop materials on inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> for examples. For basic plotting of just the mesh,
ggplot() + gg(mesh)
should do it, but it can also map functions defined on the mesh vertices, etc.

I can see the benefit of having an explicit object conversion though. I’ll put it on my list...

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Change of support for log-Gaussian Cox process model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Change of support for log-Gaussian Cox process model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Yes, in principle this type of model should be possible with inlabru. The difficulty lies in being able to express the predictor/likelihood for the areal observations. We have been thinking of how to best allow the user to express this in the interface; a SpatialPolygonsDataFrame with the counts for each polygon seems the obvious way, but we haven’t implemented this yet.

 It is almost certainly already possible to explicitly construct the required expression as a generic bru() model, since one “only” needs to express the log-integral
\log \int Lambda(s) ds,
for each polygon, which would feed directly into a regular Poisson count likelihood. The integration scheme can use the same ipoints() construction as the lgcp() models use. I just haven’t had time to test that properly, as we’ve been workin in getting the internal backend code updated so we can support the full range of latent models. I recall running into some complication for how to write the code in a general way, likely relating to the way inlabru indata is handled (it will be easier to handle as a special likelihood within inlabru than by the user in the predictor). I’m happy to discuss this further off-list.

Finn

Any advice on how to proceed?

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
You were on the right track with a basic error, but it wasn't that one.  It turns out the issue was a manifestation of a classic screw-up: never test equality on floats.  When I switch "week" to an integer type from a float, it ran. My guess is "group" was failing because grouping floats isn't guaranteed to work.  Granted, now it throws a warning:

Warning in inla(formula, family = "binomial", data = data, Ntrials = data$nsamples, : f(location, ...): Number of unused groups >= the number of groups used: 42 >= 30, this is *usually* a misspesification

But this is a good thing as I can go back to figuring out if what I'm doing makes sense and not wrestling with not being able to do it at all.

Thanks again for your help. I'm new to INLA and this is an excellent support group.

--Mike

El jue., 3 ene. 2019 a las 9:50, <harr...@mobike.com> escribió:

> `sparklyr::spark_apply` function seems can replace `mcapply` function to parallel INLA program, I am new bees for INLA, but mastering more about sparklyr. Does anyone be interesting in this?

>
> On Monday, August 10, 2015 at 7:20:36 PM UTC+8, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio wrote:

> > Hi,
> >
> > I know that this is a "cold" thread but I would like to share some thoughts on this. We have done some work to fit unimplemented models in R-INLA by fitting several models with R-INLA where some parameters had been fixed (so that the model could be fitted with R-INLA) and then combining all the resulting models using Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA).
> >
> > The idea is that if we have a model that is not implemented in R-INLA but that could be fitted by fixing one or a few parameters, then we could take different values of this ensemble of parameters over a grid, fit the conditional models (on the values of these parameters) and then combine them together using BMA. If the model is already available in R-INLA it may be faster to run simpler models and then combine them, depending on the amount of data we have.
> >

messages.subject: Generating INLA meshes from shape files in R
messages.subject_clean: Generating INLA meshes from shape files in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm new to INLA and have been using it to develop a marine species distribution model.

While building my model, I've written a couple of functions to speed up generating meshes from global shape files and then plotting them in R using ggplot2. I thought other INLA users may find the functions useful, so I've wrapped them into a package and posted it to GitHub:
https://github.com/jamesgrecian/mapr

Essentially, given a set of points (i.e. animal locations) and a buffer around the area of interest, the function will load a global shapefile from the Natural Earth database and manipulate it either for plotting as a land mask, or for passing to the inla.mesh.2d function. After chatting with Haakon Bakka, I've set an argument in the mesh creation function that allows you to switch a Neumann boundary condition on and off as required.

Please feel free to use the package, and please let me know if it is helpful in your work.

Best wishes,

James

1)
In the README example, you're not using the CRS when calling
inla.mesh.2d. Telling inla.mesh.2d what your projection is will allow
later operations with sp objects to do the right thing (e.g.
auto-convert latlong to UTM etc).  sf support isn't available yet, but
once we have time for that those features should be automatically
avaiable as well; looks like some of your sf-code may be helpful for
that! (PS. do you know if sf properly supports +proj=geocent? sp
supports it for SpatialPoints but not polygons, which is annoying but
can be worked around, but I haven't seen any geocent (i.e. xyz
Euclidean coordinates for the sphere) examples at all using sf.)

2)
The mesh itself doesn't know about boundary conditions; that's handled
by whatever model is defined on the mesh later, such as
inla.spde2.pcmatern. (Exception: 1D meshes can be constructed so the
basis functions themselves impose boundary conditions)
>From the help text of "meshr", I'm guessing that setting it to TRUE
gives a mesh extension, and FALSE doesn't?

\item{Neumann}{TRUE - returns a list to allow a Neumann boundary to be
implemented \cr
FALSE - returns a single object defining the coastline}
}

The spde models currently implemented will give Neumann boundaries in
both those cases, but in the FALSE case the Neumann condition will be
on the coastline itself, and for TRUE it will be on the extended
boundary, which is the opposite of what the help text implies!  As a
user, I would have expected Neumann=TRUE to give me Neumann coundition
on the coastline, and FALSE, to add an extension so that the Neumann
condition is moved away from the domain of interest.
Ongoing research will also result in options for other boundary
conditions, so I would suggest renaming your Neumann option and/or
clarifying the help text.

Finn

Hi Finn,

1. I'll edit the readme.md file to illustrate how you can include the CRS argument in the call to inla.mesh.2d. It was just meant as an illustration of how to pass the output of meshr to the inla.mesh.2d call.

I've been working with sf for a wee while, and have tried to move all my old scripts to use sf as much as possible. One of the driving forces was how much easier manipulating projections in plots has become with the geom_sf function for ggplot. I would be happy to help if I can, feel free to use any of the code in the package or help files. After a quick look I think sf may support "+proj=geocent", but I'm not familiar with it. Have a look at the attached: https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/issues/103

2. Sorry, I didn't explain myself very well in the post.

When Neumann = T the output of the meshr function is a list of spatial polygons. This list can then be passed to the inla.mesh.2d function and is ordered so that the Neumann condition is placed on the coastline, and there are no mesh nodes on land. This could be useful if you wanted to prevent any estimation on land at all.

When Neumann = F the output of meshr is a single spatial polygon object. When this object is then passed to inla.mesh.2d the Neumann condition is placed on the buffer region not the coastline, and there are mesh nodes on land. This allows the resulting mesh to be passed to the barrier model for example.

Thanks for your comments, I'll edit the readme.md file to make some of this clearer.

A couple of developments I was considering, if they would be of use to the community (?), would be:
1. To add options for higher resolution shape files to be downloaded for users that are working on studies at a smaller spatial scale, or;
2. To add an option for a marine vs terrestrial switch for users studying land-based systems.

Best,

James

Hi,
the Neumann parameter explanation still sounds backwards; for the
barrier model, one needs the coastline to be its own polygon, and the
outer boundary needs to be its own polygon, so there's a list of two
polygons.  But you say Neumann=FALSE gives only a single polygon.
However, looking again at the readme example figure, what you've done
there is use the coastline to cut the mesh, so that one can indeed get
a Neumann boundary on it, and that can be done by giving a set of
polygons as the second list element to inla.mesh.2d(boundary=...);
inla.mesh.2d will use the intersection as the domain definition.  I
couldn't quite tell from looking at the internals of your code if
you're doing that step there instead.
But for the barrier model one tends to want the opposite; one _wants_
to have mesh nodes on land, and the coastline use as "interior

that is confusing, since it seems to contradict how we usually use
inla.mesh.2d to do these things "by hand".

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] coercing inla.mesh to Spatial* object
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I've made a quick version of a mesh-to-Spatial* conversion function,
inla.mesh2sp. See code below.
It outputs SpatialPolygonsDataFrame (for the triangles) and
SpatialPoints (for just the vertices).
Including a special object for just the domain polygon is harder, but
we have internal code in the
'excursions' package that I could covert to work with this new function.
Is this the sort of thing you had in mind? Can you give it a try and
send me comments, and then I'll add it to the package.

Finn

#' Convert inla.mesh to sp objects
#'
#' @param mesh An \code{\link{inla.mesh}} object
#' @return A list with \code{sp} objects for triangles and vertices:
#' \describe{
#'   \item{triangles}{\code{SpatialPolygonsDataFrame} object with the
triangles in
#'   the same order as in the original mesh, but each triangle looping through
#'   the vertices in clockwise order (\code{sp} standard) instead of
#'   counterclockwise order (\code{inla.mesh} standard). The \code{data.frame}
#'   contains the vertex indices for each triangle, which is needed to link to
#'   functions defined on the vertices of the triangulation.
#'   \item{vertices}{\code{SpatialPoints} object with the vertex coordinates,
#'   in the same order as in the original mesh.}
#' }
#' @export
inla.mesh2sp <- function(mesh) {
  crs <- inla.CRS(inla.CRSargs(mesh$crs))
  isgeocentric <- identical(inla.as.list.CRS(crs)[["proj"]], "geocent")
  if (isgeocentric || (mesh$manifold == "S2")) {
    stop(paste0(
      "'sp' doesn't support storing polygons in geocentric coordinates.\n",
      "Convert to a map projection with inla.spTransform() before
calling inla.mesh2sp()."))
  }

  triangles <- SpatialPolygonsDataFrame(
    Sr = SpatialPolygons(lapply(
      1:nrow(mesh$graph$tv),
      function(x) {
        tv <- mesh$graph$tv[x, , drop = TRUE]
        Polygons(list(Polygon(mesh$loc[tv[c(1, 3, 2, 1)],
                                       1:2,
                                       drop = FALSE])),
                 ID = x)
      }
    ),
    proj4string = crs
    ),
    data = as.data.frame(mesh$graph$tv[, c(1, 3, 2), drop = FALSE]),
    match.ID = FALSE
  )
  vertices <- SpatialPoints(mesh$loc[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], proj4string = crs)

  list(triangles = triangles, vertices = vertices)
}

See the code below. The trick is to use the exact same prior (model) in both cases to get the same results:

Note that NEITHER of these are recommended options. What I would recommend is same/similar to what you use as m2:
>> data$expkd_t<-((y/(2*pi*(x^2)*base::gamma(2/y)))*exp(-(data$distance^y/(x^y))))*1E5

-----

#Dataset
data=as.data.frame(matrix(c(0,0,0,0,0,1,3,1,2,2,1,1,2,1,2,20,25,12,11,1,20,20,6,10,8,3,4,10,5,4,500,300,140,600,200,160,200,150,130,160,120,98,45,20,35),ncol=3))
names(data) <- c("s","trials","distance")

#Exponential power kernel
x=230;y=3
data$expkd<-((y/(2*pi*(x^2)*base::gamma(2/y)))*exp(-(data$distance^y/(x^y))))
data$expkd_t<-((y/(2*pi*(x^2)*base::gamma(2/y)))*exp(-(data$distance^y/(x^y))))*10000

#Models

m1<-inla(s ~ 1 + expkd, data=data, Ntrials=trials,family="binomial",
         control.fixed = list(prec = 1E-3),
         control.predictor = list(compute=T)) # ppd sd to the prior sd
m2<-inla(s ~ 1 + expkd_t, data=data, Ntrials=trials,family="binomial",
         control.fixed = list(prec = 1E5),
         control.predictor = list(compute=T)) # correct sd
# Using 1E5 = 1E-3 * (1E-4)^(-2)
summary(m1)
summary(m2)

## Similar
summary(m1$summary.fixed$`0.5quant`[2]*data$expkd)
summary(m2$summary.fixed$`0.5quant`[2]*data$expkd_t)

summary(m1$summary.linear.predictor$mean)
summary(m2$summary.linear.predictor$mean)

plot(m1$summary.linear.predictor$mean, data$s/data$trials)
plot(m2$summary.linear.predictor$mean, data$s/data$trials)
-----

messages.body_plain:
Sorry that should say current stable release of INLA installed today - not BLAS !
James

On Wednesday, January 9, 2019 at 5:04:56 PM UTC, jpkrooney wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I hope this question is not too vague. I have been trying to rerun an inla model I first developed 3 or 4 years ago. I haven't changed any of the R script code or inla model specification. I am on a new hexcore macbook vs my old quad core one. Because its anew machine I also reinstalled software so I'm on newer versions of MacOS (Mojave), R (3.5.1), BLAS, (Current stable release installed today), etc. I have mostly been doing other work and so I've not been keeping up with the developments in INLA - I'm conscious many things could have changed that I'm unaware of.
>
> My model has quite a large graph - about 55,000 nodes. Previously it run in about 15-16 minutes using the same data. Now, R code runs fine, inla appears to start fine, producing the messages below. However, the model is taking along time to run (45mins and counting).
>
> My model code is:
> # Define INLA formulae
> formula.allcases = obTOT ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph="nb.sa.txt",
>                                  hyper = list(prec.unstruct = list(param = c(1,0.0001)),
>                                               prec.spatial = list(param=c(1,0.1))))
>
> mod1 <- inla(formula.allcases, data=data1, family="poisson", E = exTOT,
>                      control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1, cdf=c(0)),
>                      control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE), verbose=TRUE)
>
> When I run it the console returns the messages below, however after 45 mins and counting I'm still waiting.
>
> Can anyone advise what I should be looking at to speed things up? I will let it continue to run so long as I don't need to do something else in the mean time to see if it comes back with errors.
>
> Thanks,
> James
>
>

> Report bugs to <he...@r-inla.org>

messages.body_plain:
It could very well be (thx Finn!) that the default integration scheme
for |theta| = 2, was at some point changed from "ccd" to "grid".
looking back, it was here:

changeset:   3172:4fae4c750a63
user:        Havard Rue <havar...@math.ntnu.no>
date:        Mon Mar 14 09:19:35 2016 +0100
files:       gmrflib/approx-inference.c
description:
Set int.strategy = auto to grid also for nhyper=2

and it might very well be this.

you can check it by 'reverting' back to the old style using argument

control.inla = list(int.strategy = "ccd")

you can also check if the new testing version runs better after setting

inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE)

(assuming you're on R-3.5)

let me know.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi Havard,

That worked thanks you. The ccd integration strategy brought the runtime down to about 10 mins. The mkl option by itself didn't seem to make much difference (at least I didn't have patient to wait for it to finish so it may have been a bit quicker but not dramatically. Doing both options together seemed to improve things a bit more taking about 9 mins.

Thanks for your help!

On Wednesday, January 9, 2019 at 7:52:43 PM UTC, Helpdesk wrote:

> It could very well be (thx Finn!) that the default integration scheme
> for |theta| = 2, was at some point changed from "ccd" to "grid".
> looking back, it was here:
>
> changeset:   3172:4fae4c750a63
> user:        Havard Rue <havar...@math.ntnu.no>
> date:        Mon Mar 14 09:19:35 2016 +0100
> files:       gmrflib/approx-inference.c
> description:
> Set int.strategy = auto to grid also for nhyper=2
>
> and it might very well be this.
>
> you can check it by 'reverting' back to the old style using argument
>
> control.inla = list(int.strategy = "ccd")
>
> you can also check if the new testing version runs better after setting
>
> inla.setOption(mkl = TRUE)
>
> (assuming you're on R-3.5)
>
> let me know.
>
> Best
> H
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Computing exceedance probability
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Computing exceedance probability
messages.body_plain:
Either use

	inla.posterior.sample()

or use linear-combinations to extract such information.

with linear combinations, you get the marginal, and you can use
inla.pmarginal()  to compute the CDF.

for linear combinations, see the FAQ at r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>

H

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

inla model running fine on RStudio on own machine fails when running on Ubuntu version 14.04.5 LTS (GNU/Linux 3.13.0-164-generic x86_64) with error "Segmentation fault (core dumped) Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed()"

Currently using INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround()

and

system(inla.getOption("inla.call"))
Segmentation fault (core dumped)

No other specification.

See model and session info below:

"form <- y ~ 0 + f(pred1, model='clinear',range=c(0,Inf),initial=0) +
                f(pred2, model='clinear',range=c(0,Inf),initial=0) +
                f(pred3, model='clinear',range=c(0,Inf),initial=0) +
                f(pred4, model='clinear',range=c(0,Inf),initial=0) +
                f(pred5, model='clinear',range=c(0,Inf),initial=0) +
                f(pred6, model='clinear',range=c(0,Inf),initial=0) +
                f(space, model = spde)

model <- inla(form,
              family = 'normal',
              data = inla.stack.data(stk.env),
              control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.env)),
              control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE),
              verbose = TRUE,
              num.threads = 60)"

messages.body_plain:

I guess the problems on Ubuntu 14.05 is because its binaries are
compiled on Ubuntu 18.04. You can try the Ubuntu 16.04 or the CentOS
builds, on http://inla.r-inla-download.org/Linux-builds/
the HOWTO file tells how.

An alternative, you can try the static version

	library(INLA)
	INLA::inla.dynload.workaround()

and check if that works on the (rather old) 14.04

H

messages.subject: bym2 inla.posterior.sample control quantization?
messages.subject_clean: bym2 inla.posterior.sample control quantization?
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA gurus.

I am working on a bym2 model. I am trying to create bivariate plots of the joint posterior of some hyperparameters (phi vs sigma in the example below) via inla.posterior.sample.  The marginals look good. However, the posterior simulations seem to be quantized/discretized. Instead, I am hoping to get a more even distribution (nondiscretized version) as one might obtain from MCMC. How might I be able to obtain a more even sample distribution? Thanks!

The example below is taken directly from the "Germany example" using bym2 obtained from (http://www.r-inla.org/examples/case-studies), more specifically:

#####################################################################
## the Germany example  http://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/case-studies/pc-prior/bym/runme.R

data(Germany)
g = "germany.graph"
n = dim(Germany)[1]
Q = INLA:::inla.pc.bym.Q(g)
Q = INLA:::inla.scale.model(Q, constr=list(A=matrix(1, 1, n), e=0))

u = 0.2/0.31
alpha = 0.01
phi.u = 0.5
phi.alpha = 2/3 ## prob(phi < phi.u) = phi.alpha

phi.prior = INLA:::inla.pc.bym.phi(Q=Q, u= phi.u, alpha = phi.alpha)
values = (-9):110
values = 1:100
bym_hyper = list(
  phi = list( prior="pc", param=c(phi.u, phi.alpha), initial = -3),
  prec = list( prior="pc.prec", param = c(u, alpha), initial = 5)
)
rw2_hyper = list(prec=list( prior="pc.prec", param=c(u, alpha)))

formula = Y ~ 1
  + f(region, model="bym2", graph=g, scale.model=TRUE, constr=TRUE, hyper=bym_hyper)
  + f(x, model="rw2", values=values, scale.model=TRUE, hyper=rw2_hyper)

r = inla(formula, data=Germany, family="poisson", E=E,
  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
  control.compute=list(config = TRUE)
)

r = r.germany = inla.hyperpar(r, dz = .5, diff.logdens=15)

## --------
## to this point, the code is identical to the tutorial/example

## simulation of joint posterior:
ps = inla.posterior.sample(n=1000, r)

hyper_names  = names(ps[[1]]$hyperpar )

i_phi = grep("Phi for region", hyper_names, fixed=TRUE )
i_sigma = grep("Precision for region", hyper_names, fixed=TRUE )

phi = sapply( ps, function(o) {o$hyperpar[[i_phi]] } )
sigma = sapply( ps, function(o) {1/sqrt(o$hyperpar[[i_sigma]])} )

# histograms are not smooth distributions
hist(phi, breaks=100 )
hist(sigma, breaks=100 )

# scatterplot I am trying to obtain .. looks to be discretized .. how to make more even
plot( phi ~ sigma )

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] bym2 inla.posterior.sample control quantization?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] bym2 inla.posterior.sample control quantization?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

with inla.posterior.sample(), only the integration points for the
hyperparameters in the INLA approximation
 are used as sample candidates.  If you need more complete samples for
the hyperparameters (but not simultaneously the latent variables), you
can use inla.hyperpar.sample() instead.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] About SPDE hyperpar : range and sd
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] About SPDE hyperpar : range and sd
messages.body_plain:
You'll need to study variograms a bit. See e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variogram

The range is the range of the variogram: the distance at which observations are more or less independent.
The sd is a measurement of the variability among pairs of points at distances (much) larger than the range.

> It outputs SpatialPolygonsDataFrame (for the triangles) and
> SpatialPoints (for just the vertices).
> Including a special object for just the domain polygon is harder, but
> we have internal code in the
> 'excursions' package that I could covert to work with this new function.
> Is this the sort of thing you had in mind? Can you give it a try and
> send me comments, and then I'll add it to the package.
>
> Finn
>
> #' Convert inla.mesh to sp objects
> #'
> #' @param mesh An \code{\link{inla.mesh}} object
> #' @return A list with \code{sp} objects for triangles and vertices:
> #' \describe{
> #'   \item{triangles}{\code{SpatialPolygonsDataFrame} object with the
> triangles in
> #'   the same order as in the original mesh, but each triangle looping through
> #'   the vertices in clockwise order (\code{sp} standard) instead of
> #'   counterclockwise order (\code{inla.mesh} standard). The \code{data.frame}
> #'   contains the vertex indices for each triangle, which is needed to link to
> #'   functions defined on the vertices of the triangulation.
> #'   \item{vertices}{\code{SpatialPoints} object with the vertex coordinates,
> #'   in the same order as in the original mesh.}
> #' }
> #' @export
> inla.mesh2sp <- function(mesh) {
>   crs <- inla.CRS(inla.CRSargs(mesh$crs))
>   isgeocentric <- identical(inla.as.list.CRS(crs)[["proj"]], "geocent")
>   if (isgeocentric || (mesh$manifold == "S2")) {
>     stop(paste0(
>       "'sp' doesn't support storing polygons in geocentric coordinates.\n",
>       "Convert to a map projection with inla.spTransform() before
> calling inla.mesh2sp()."))
>   }
>
>   triangles <- SpatialPolygonsDataFrame(
>     Sr = SpatialPolygons(lapply(
>       1:nrow(mesh$graph$tv),
>       function(x) {
>         tv <- mesh$graph$tv[x, , drop = TRUE]
>         Polygons(list(Polygon(mesh$loc[tv[c(1, 3, 2, 1)],
>                                        1:2,
>                                        drop = FALSE])),
>                  ID = x)
>       }
>     ),
>     proj4string = crs
>     ),
>     data = as.data.frame(mesh$graph$tv[, c(1, 3, 2), drop = FALSE]),
>     match.ID = FALSE
>   )
>   vertices <- SpatialPoints(mesh$loc[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], proj4string = crs)
>
>   list(triangles = triangles, vertices = vertices)
> }

messages.subject: Question about the weights option
messages.subject_clean: Question about the weights option
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

So I'm thinking to build a model with simulated data, and I was wondering could I use weights. Essentially, I'm simulate case control data where the cases are rare. Lets say I might have 2000 controls for each case. I could simulate 2000 controls with essentially the same variables, but I was wondering could I simulate 1 control and weight it x2000 relative to the 1 case - hopefully this would be faster when I have 1000 cases and 2 million controls for example. Anyhow, I was looking at the documentation and found the following dire warnings about weights:

> Fixed (optional) weights parameters of the likelihood, so the log-likelihood[i] is changed into weights[i]*log-likelihood[i]. Default value is rep(1, n.data). Due to the danger of mis-interpreting the results (see below), this option is DISABLED by default. You can enable this option for the rest of your R session, doing inla.setOption(enable.inla.argument.weights=TRUE). WARNING: The normalizing constant for the likelihood is NOT recomputed, so ALL marginals (and the marginal likelihood) must be interpreted with great care. Possibly, you may want to set the prior for the hyperparameters to "uniform" and the integration strategy to "eb" to mimic a maximum-likelihood approach.

Weighting the likelihood sounds like what I want to do, but I'm not sure what "interpreted with great care" implies ? My best guess is this is due to the normalising constant not being recomputed so therefore model parameters are off ? What is the advantage of setting uniform priors and the "eb" integrations strategy ?

I hope this question makes sense - apologies if not I'm still thinking this through

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about the weights option
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Question about the weights option
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

2000 simulated data points is _not_ equivalent to 1 data point with
weight 2000, since you'd be leaving out all the random variability
between the samples and amplifying the one single data point. Yes, it
would be faster, but I'd expect the results to be very very wrong.
Otherwise we'd be doing this all the time; why use a large data set if
you could simply take a single data point and repeat it with no ill
effect? Consider a sample x_1,...,x_n ~ N(mu, sigma^2).  How would you
estimate the variance sigma^2 if you only used x_1, with likelihood
weighted by a factor n? It would be equivalent to just repeating x_1 n
times, which would give empirical variance exactly equal to zero.
Clearly not right.

The uniform+eb comment is there due to the most common use case of
"weights" is to mimic a certain frequentistic method, and that makes
it close to that.

Finn

Yes good point, but perhaps I didn't' explain very well.

I'm working with a BYM2 model with about 2200 cases from a population of 4million over 23 years. (although I could calculate a more complex weight including the national population of 40-45yr females and the per polygon population of 40-45yr females).

Anyway, thanks for your answer!

Hello! I am a beginner in R-inla and am building a spatial binomial model to predict the presence and absence of an aquatic plant species. Here is my code, pieced together from reading many different tutorials and from the Zuur book from 2017:

#create mesh
mesh1 <- inla.mesh.create.helper(points=cbind(total.final.mini$x,total.final.mini$y),max.edge=c(500,2000),cutoff=0,offset=c(10,140),min.angle=c(26,21))

#matern spde model object
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh1,alpha=2)

#coordinates as a matrix
coords <- as.matrix(total.final.mini[,1:2])

#Construct observation/prediction weight matrices based on mesh
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh1,loc=coords)

#list of named index vectors for SPDE model
time.index <- inla.spde.make.index("coordinates", n.spde = spde$n.spde)

#build the stack
stack3 <- inla.stack(data=list(y = total.final.mini$pres, link=1, Ntrials=1),
                     A=list(A,1),
                     effects=list(c(time.index),
                                  data.frame(Intercept=1,total.final.mini[,5:6])),tag="est")

#formula
formula3 <- y ~ 0 + Intercept +
  neighbors + total.area +
  f(coordinates, model=spde)

#data object
data = inla.stack.data(stack3)

#call to inla
r3 <- inla(formula3, family="binomial",Ntrials=1,
           data=data,control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T),
           control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack3),compute=TRUE,link=1,
                                  quantiles=c(0.025,0.5,0.975)))

#look at posterior distributions
summary(r3)

I am confused because all the posterior values for one of my fixed effects (total area) is all zeros. This doesn't make sense to me, because this fixed effect ranges from 0 to 19500000 (units are meters).

Do you have any idea why I would get all zeros here? Thank you! Any insights are much appreciated.

messages.body_plain:
If the effect of that covariate is small, say less than 1, the coefficient needs to be small to scale down the large range. The summary output shows the estimated coefficient, not the combined effect.  Try scaling down total.area by a factor 1e6 and see if that makes a difference.

Also look at $summary.fixed to avoid pretty-printing artifacts. (Rounding to 4 digits is too harsh if the estimate is 1e-7!)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a model with about 50,000 rows of data, which I use for training, and then about 100 rows of data I want to predict outcomes for.

As part of evaluating model fit, I'm drawing samples from the posterior and analyzing fit for the "test data" rows.  However, sampling for all 50,000 rows is extremely slow, and takes much longer than fitting the actual model.

The command I use is:

inla.posterior.sample(10000, model)

Two questions related to this:
1) Is there a way to *only* sample from the 100 rows I'm interested in for testing?  (Should be significantly faster)
2) I see that Inla returns posterior samples for everything, not just my dependent variable.  To be sure that I always extract things cleanly, is there a definitive way to select the correct posterior samples from the INLA command output?  (i.e. rows 1-100 are dependent variable, row 101 is beta_1, row 102 is beta_2, etc...)

Thank You!

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 2019-01-16 at 21:23 -0800, Bayes2 wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I have a model with about 50,000 rows of data, which I use for
> training, and then about 100 rows of data I want to predict outcomes
> for.

I guess adding NA's in the response for these does not work in your
case, and that you have to do some kind of simulation.

> inla.posterior.sample(10000, model)

Since the model is represented with its precision matrix, we cannot 'just sample a subset'
of the latent 'x', we have to sample the whole 'x' and then extract the subset 'x[sub]'

Instead of returning the whole sample, which takes a lot of storage, there is an additional
argument (at least in the most recent testing versions),

selection: Select what part of the sample to return. By default, the
          whole sample is returned. ‘selection’ is a named list with
          the name of the components of the sample, and what indices of
          them to return. Names include ‘APredictor’, ‘Predictor’,
          ‘(Intercept)’, and otherwise names in the formula.  The
          values of the list, is interpreted as indices. If they are
          negative, they are interpreted as 'not', a zero is
          interpreted as 'all', and positive indices are interpreted as
          'only'. The names of elements of each samples refer to the
          indices in the full sample.

so you can define which ones to return. this will reduce the storage, not the sampling time.

Another way to sample from x[sub], is to compute in some way the marginal joint distribution for 'x[sub]' and
then sample from it 'manually'.

This can be done, conditionally, or unconditionally on the hyperparameters.

Unconditionally.

By defining a linear combination, one for each component in x[sub], you can set this one to TRUE,

lincomb.derived.correlation.matrix: Logical If TRUE compute also the
          correlations for the derived linear combinations, if FALSE do
          not (Default FALSE)

in 'control.inla'. this will return, on result$misc, the posterior correlation matrix of the all
the linear combinations. Since this, by construction, happens to be your 'x[sub]', you know the copula,
and the marginals, and you can generate samples from the joint.

Conditionally.

This is a little more involved, and in this case, we have to go through the stored configurations with config=TRUE,
and solve |sub| linear systems to get the conditionally covariance for x[sub], and then... This is to much internal stuff
maybe best if it all was wrapped up as a function in the package...

H

--
Håvard Rue
Helpdesk
he...@r-inla.org

messages.body_plain:
Yes, you need to compute the relative risk yourself, unless you're
happy with the E*exp(\eta) one, which is just a scaled version of the
Expected value when you include the zero-inflation.

You can extract the zero-probability from the fit, yes.

Strictly, there is a dependence of the zero-prob and the linear
predictor, and if you want/need to account for that, you have to rely
on using inla.posterior.sample, like this small example

data(Germany)
g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
source(system.file("demodata/Bym-map.R", package="INLA"))
form = Y ~ f(region,model="besag",graph=g)
r  =  inla(form, family="zeroinflatedpoisson1", data=Germany, E=E,
           control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

ysim.fun = function(...)
{
    args = list(...)
    prob = theta[1]
    n = length(Predictor)
    return (prob + (1-prob) * rpois(n, lambda = args$E *
exp(Predictor)))
}
xx = inla.posterior.sample(10000, r)
yy = inla.posterior.sample.eval(ysim.fun, xx, E=Germany$E)
y.mean = apply(yy,1,mean)
germany.map(y.mean/Germany$E)

messages.body_plain:
Note that that code won't give you samples from the posterior; only
samples for which the posterior expectation (I believe) is correct,
but the variance etc will not be.
For full posterior samples one needs to sample a 0/1 variable for the
zero inflation:

rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 1-prob) * rpois(n, lambda = ...)

Since the zero-probability is constant, I wouldn't expect that to
change the spatial pattern; only the general variability.

(I'm involved with a project where zero-inflated poisson likelihood
interacts with multiple random effects, where we are looking at a
variance reduced, Rao-Blackwellised version, for the posterior mean
and variance, but it's not publicly available yet.)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I'm confused on setting priors for bym2. I know how code it, but I don't have a good intuition on what the numbers mean. However, when I plot a map based on a model with default bym2 priors it tends to look speckled, which I think might imply my priors are not properly calibrated for the iid vs besag elements of my model.

My model specified like so:
formula.allcases.bym2 = obTOT ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym2", graph="nb.sa.txt")
mod.allcases <- inla(formula.allcases.bym2, data=as.data.frame(SA), family="poisson", E = exTOT,
                         control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1, cdf=c(0)),
                         control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, config = TRUE), verbose=TRUE, num.threads = 10,
                     control.inla = list(int.strategy = "ccd") )

The map of RR's tends to look speckled as I said (small section but its throughout the map):

And a plot of the hyperparameters with priors shown looks like this:

I've tried changing the pc prior:
formula.allcases.bym2 = obTOT ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym2", graph="nb.sa.txt",
                                      hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param = c(1, 0.001))))
but it made little difference.
I know that prior = "pc" is the mixing parameter phi with default (0.5, 0.5), but I don''t know in what way i should change it. In particular how do I need to change both 0.5's or just one ?
thanks for any advice!

messages.subject_clean: Question about inla.posterior.sample
messages.body_plain:
Hello! I have a spatial binomial model and am trying to conduct bootstrap analysis using inla.posterior.sample. However, I am confused about how to move forward to get the probabilities. Here is what I have so far:

#build the mesh using x and y coordinates
mesh1 <- inla.mesh.create.helper(points=cbind(total.final.mini$x,total.final.mini$y),max.edge=c(500,2000),cutoff=0,offset=c(10,140),min.angle=c(26,21))

coords <- as.matrix(total.final.mini[,1:2])set.seed(12345)

#matern spde model object
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh1,alpha=2)

#coordinates as a matrix
coords <- as.matrix(total.final.mini[,1:2])

#Construct observation/prediction weight matrices based on mesh
A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh1,loc=coords)

#list of named index vectors for SPDE model
time.index <- inla.spde.make.index("coordinates", n.spde = spde$n.spde)

#standardize covariates
library(RegularizedSCA)

total.final.mini$neighbors.std <- (total.final.mini$neighbors - mean(total.final.mini$neighbors)) / sd(total.final.mini$neighbors)
total.final.mini$total.area.std <- (total.final.mini$total.area - mean(total.final.mini$total.area)) / sd(total.final.mini$total.area)

N <- nrow(total.final.mini)

X <- data.frame(Intercept=rep(1,N), total.final.mini$neighbors.std, total.final.mini$total.area.std)

colnames(X) <- c("Intercept","neighbors.std", "total.area.std")

#build the stack
stack3 <- inla.stack(data=list(y = total.final.mini$pres, link=1, Ntrials=1),
                     A=list(A,1),
                     effects=list(w=time.index,
                                  X=as.data.frame(X)),tag="est")

#formula
formula3 <- y ~ -1 + Intercept +
  neighbors.std + total.area.std +
  f(coordinates, model=spde)

#data object
data = inla.stack.data(stack3)

#call to inla
r3 <- inla(formula3, family="binomial",Ntrials=1,
           data=data,control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=T,config=T),
           control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack3),compute=TRUE,link=1,
                                  quantiles=c(0.025,0.5,0.975)))

#call inla.posterior.sample to generate one value for each of the parameters
Sim <- inla.posterior.sample(n=1,result=r3, seed=12345)

#names of my parameters
MyParams <- c("Intercept","neighbors.std","total.area.std")

#find out the row numbers for the regression parameters within the Sim object
rownum <- lapply(MyParams, function(x) grep(x,rownames(Sim[[1]]$latent),fixed=T))

rownum <- as.numeric(rownum)

#access the simulated values of the three parameters (betas) from Sim[[1]]$latent
Betas <- Sim[[1]]$latent[as.numeric(rownum)]

#we also need the simulated spatial random field (w) values. These are in:
w <- Sim[[1]]$latent[1029:2386]
head(w)

#make covariate dataframe into a matrix
Xm <- as.matrix(X)
#make A into a matrix
Am <- as.matrix(A)
dim(A)

#we can now calculate the fitted values based on the simulated parameter values
FixedPart <- Xm %*% Betas
SpatialPart <- Am %*% w

#next I want to use these simulated parameter values to simulate the response (0's and 1's) and I believe I should use rbinom, but I don't know how to get the probabilities (I assume I should do something with FixedPart and SpatialPart but not sure what.

Ysim <- rbinom(n=nrow(total.final.mini), size=1, prob=?)

Thank you!!

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In Section 7.2, the model is almost the same as in Cameletti et al; an
AR(1) process in time on the temporal basis functions, kronecker with
a 2D SPDE in space.
The difference is that in Cameletti et al, the knots were integers
equal to the timepoints.  In 7.2 and 7.3of the book, other knot
placements are used. The knot choice in 7.2 actually does looks a bit
odd, but perhaps it makes sense when comparing to the time values of
the data. In 7.3., fewer knots than data timepoints are used, to
reduce the model resolution and therefore reduce the computational
cost.

Finn

messages.subject: INLA SPDE model: How to define the stack for a regression model with spatially varying coefficients
messages.subject_clean: INLA SPDE model: How to define the stack for a regression model with spatially varying coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I am currently learning how to use the SPDE approach and try to apply this approach to my data.
However, for this particular problem, I have not yet found an example and would thus kindly ask for advice.
I have data of 1.6 million individuals which are distributed across 8850 neighbourhoods (centroid coordinates). My reponse variable is available for each individual (yes = 1, no = 0) , some explanatory variables are also at the individual level and some aggregated at the neighbourhood level.
I would like to create a SPDE model where two variables are global and two variables are allowed to vary over space and create a continuous surface of the respective coefficient estimates. I know how to fit a comparable model with areal data, but given the fine resolution of the neighbourhoods, a continuous surface would probably look much better here for the coefficient estimates.

The formula itself for a logistic regression model should look this way:

formula <- response ~ -1 + intercept  + a + b  + f(c, spatial.field, model=spde) + f(d, spatial.field, model = spde)

where a and b are global variables, c and d are spatially varying variables, for which I want to create the raster surface.

This is what I have done so far:

### Create the mesh (not shown)

## Combine the data points with the mesh:

A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh2, loc=cbind(data$X, data$Y))
dim(A)

#### create the spatial index:

s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field",
                                n.spde=spde$n.spde)

s.index$spatial.field = seq(1,spde$n.spde)
s.index$spatial.field.group = rep(1,spde$n.spde)
s.index$spatial.field.repl = rep(1,spde$n.spde)

### Create the stack with the dependent variable and the expl. variables - this is obviously wrong, but I don`t get any further:

stack.est <- inla.stack(data=list(response=data$response),
                        A=list(A),
                        effects=list(c(s.index, effects=list(intercept=1,
                                                           a = data$a, b = data$b, c = data$c,
                                                           d = data$d))),  tag="est")

####### Create a raster to predict the coefficients onto

basic_raster <- raster(ncol = 500, nrow = 500, xmn = 33206888, xmx = 33483784,
                       ymn = 5690480, ymx = 6060859)
basic_raster

projection(basic_raster) <- "+proj=tmerc +lat_0=0 +lon_0=15 +k=0.9996 +x_0=33500000 +y_0=0 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs"

coo <- coordinates(basic_raster)

### create the A matrix to calculate the coefficients at these rasters

A.pred6 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh2, loc=as.matrix(coo))
dim(A.pred6)

##### create the stack for the prediction of the coefficient surface - i.e. at the rasters, where I don`t have values observed

stack.pred.response <- inla.stack(data=list(response=NA),
                                  A=list(A.pred6),
                                  effects=list(c(s.index, list(intercept=1))),
                                  tag="pred.response")

## join all stacks together

join.stack <- inla.stack(stack.est, stack.pred.response)

#### this should be the formula

formula <- response ~ -1 + intercept  + a + b +  + f(c, spatial.field, model=spde) + f(d, spatial.field, model = spde)

## and this is the INLA call

join.output <- inla(formula,  control.compute = list(dic=T),
                    data=inla.stack.data(join.stack),
                    family = "binomial",
                    control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(join.stack),
                                           compute=TRUE, quantiles=NULL),
                    control.results=list(return.marginals.random=FALSE,
                                         return.marginals.predictor=FALSE), verbose = T,
                    control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"))

summary(join.output)

Here are my questions for the experts:

1. Obviously the definition of the stack is wrong and I get errors. How should I define the stack for my undertaking in particular?

2. To create the continuous surface of the coefficient estimates, is it correct to create a stack with the response = NA and join this with the other stacks?

3. Where / how can I extract the coefficient estimates of the rasters after it has calculated?

I would like to thank you very much in advance and also would like to thank you for the commitment to the INLA project and your great help, which motivated me to dig even deeper.

Best wishes,

Boris

> Dear INLA experts,
>
> I am currently learning how to use the SPDE approach and try to apply
> this approach to my data.
> However, for this particular problem, I have not yet found an example
> and would thus kindly ask for advice.
> I have data of 1.6 million individuals which are distributed across
> 8850 neighbourhoods (centroid coordinates). My reponse variable is
> available for each individual (yes = 1, no = 0) , some explanatory
> variables are also at the individual level and some aggregated at the
> neighbourhood level.
> I would like to create a SPDE model where two variables are global
> and two variables are allowed to vary over space and create a
> continuous surface of the respective coefficient estimates. I know
> how to fit a comparable model with areal data, but given the fine
> resolution of the neighbourhoods, a continuous surface would probably
> look much better here for the coefficient estimates.
>
> The formula itself for a logistic regression model should look this
> way:
>
> formula <- response ~ -1 + intercept  + a + b  + f(c, spatial.field,
> model=spde) + f(d, spatial.field, model = spde)
>
> where a and b are global variables, c and d are spatially varying
> variables, for which I want to create the raster surface.
>
> This is what I have done so far:
>
> ### Create the mesh (not shown)
>
> ## Combine the data points with the mesh:
>
> A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh2, loc=cbind(data$X, data$Y))
> dim(A)
>
> #### create the spatial index:
>
>
> s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field",
>                                 n.spde=spde$n.spde)
>
> s.index$spatial.field = seq(1,spde$n.spde)
> s.index$spatial.field.group = rep(1,spde$n.spde)
> s.index$spatial.field.repl = rep(1,spde$n.spde)
>
> ### Create the stack with the dependent variable and the expl.
> variables - this is obviously wrong, but I don`t get any further:
>
> stack.est <- inla.stack(data=list(response=data$response),
>                         A=list(A),
>                         effects=list(c(s.index,
> effects=list(intercept=1,
>                                                            a =
> data$a, b = data$b, c = data$c,
>                                                            d =
> data$d))),  tag="est")
>
> ####### Create a raster to predict the coefficients onto
>
> basic_raster <- raster(ncol = 500, nrow = 500, xmn = 33206888, xmx =
> 33483784,
>                        ymn = 5690480, ymx = 6060859)
> basic_raster
>
> projection(basic_raster) <- "+proj=tmerc +lat_0=0 +lon_0=15 +k=0.9996
> +x_0=33500000 +y_0=0 +ellps=GRS80 +units=m +no_defs"
>
> coo <- coordinates(basic_raster)
>
> ### create the A matrix to calculate the coefficients at these
> rasters
>
> A.pred6 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh2, loc=as.matrix(coo))
> dim(A.pred6)
>
> ##### create the stack for the prediction of the coefficient surface
> - i.e. at the rasters, where I don`t have values observed
>
> stack.pred.response <- inla.stack(data=list(response=NA),
>                                   A=list(A.pred6),
>                                   effects=list(c(s.index,
> list(intercept=1))),
>                                   tag="pred.response")
>
> ## join all stacks together
>
>
> join.stack <- inla.stack(stack.est, stack.pred.response)
>
> #### this should be the formula
>
> formula <- response ~ -1 + intercept  + a + b +  + f(c,
> spatial.field, model=spde) + f(d, spatial.field, model = spde)
>
> ## and this is the INLA call
>
> join.output <- inla(formula,  control.compute = list(dic=T),
>                     data=inla.stack.data(join.stack),
>                     family = "binomial",
>
> control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(join.stack),
>                                            compute=TRUE,
> quantiles=NULL),
>
> control.results=list(return.marginals.random=FALSE,
>
> return.marginals.predictor=FALSE), verbose = T,
>                     control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian",
> int.strategy = "eb"))
>
> summary(join.output)
>
> Here are my questions for the experts:
>
> 1. Obviously the definition of the stack is wrong and I get errors.
> How should I define the stack for my undertaking in particular?
>
> 2. To create the continuous surface of the coefficient estimates, is
> it correct to create a stack with the response = NA and join this
> with the other stacks?
>
> 3. Where / how can I extract the coefficient estimates of the rasters
> after it has calculated?
>
> I would like to thank you very much in advance and also would like to
> thank you for the commitment to the INLA project and your great help,
> which motivated me to dig even deeper.
>
> Best wishes,
>

messages.body_plain:
you can also check out any book on timeseries, with

x_t = phi * x_t + eps_t

then at stationarity,

Var(x) = phi^2 * Var(x) + Var(eps)

and there you go...
